transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-20
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~75 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Samir Kapoor (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Apogee - Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (Apogee - Platform), Ravi Patel (Apogee - SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Redwood ran through a proposed benchmark playbook to make apples-to-apples comparisons between hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem stacks. Focus areas: prompt canonicalization, deterministic seed lists, load generator configuration (ramp, steady, burst), KV cache cold/warm cycles, batching profiles, and quantization impact. Customer asked about VPC peering, network egress, and auditability. Agreed to provision pilot and run 3 canonical workloads.

Topics:
- Prompt set curation and seeding
- Load generation: ramp/steady/pulse profiles
- KV cache warmup & consistency checks
- Batching (latency vs throughput tradeoffs)
- Quantization matrix (FP16/INT8/QLoRa?) and measuring quality drift
- VPC/on-prem network considerations and data plane isolation

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll kick us off, this is Jordan from Redwood. We put together a short playbook for running apples-to-apples benchs -- uh apologies, benchs, benchmarking across hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:15] Carlos: Thanks Jordan. We're particularly worried about the end-to-end tail latency for conversational flows. Also costs — we need real numbers.
[00:28] Samir: Totally. Today we'll walk through a lab runbook: prompt canonicalization, load profiles, and a consistent scoring rubric for quality. We'll also show KV-cache and batching experiments.
[00:42] Sofia: For context, our infra is hybrid — cloud plus some on-prem hardware for sensitive PII workloads. We can open VPC peering to Redwood dedicated pools for the pilot. Network team is Ravi.
[00:55] Ravi: Yep I can do peering, need CIDRs and a runbook of ports. Also need to know if there's any egress for logs.
[01:06] Jordan: Great. High-level plan: 1) agree canonical prompt sets and failure criteria; 2) provision three environments (Redwood hosted, Redwood dedicated in customer VPC, and customer-onprem instance or equivalent); 3) run three workload profiles with deterministic seeds; 4) capture token-level latencies, tail p95/p99, throughput, and model quality metrics.
[01:28] Carlos: How do you ensure the prompts are identical? Small tokenization differences can change results.
[01:35] Lina: Good question. We canonicalize by normalizing whitespace, unicode NFKC, and by running tokenizer parity checks. We also include a seed hash for each prompt.
[01:47] Sofia: Will you share the tokenizer version as well?
[01:50] Samir: Yes, we include the model tokenizer version and a small script to generate the hashed canonical prompt. It's in the runbook link — see shared drive: https://redwood-internal.s3/bench/runbook-apogee (note: link is placeholder).
[02:05] Ravi: Ok. On caching: how do you measure KV cache effects? We saw big improvements previously but not sure of warm vs cold patterns.
[02:13] Samir: We do a 3-phase approach: cold-start (no cache), warm (populate prefix cache with synthetic warmups), and steady-state with random session interleaving. We also run controlled cache-eviction tests to measure degradation. Each phase has a defined warmup period and metrics collection window.
[02:33] Jordan: And we recommend running 5 repeats for statistical significance and aggregating token-level timings.
[02:40] Carlos: For quantization, what knobs do you include? We've got models floating between FP16 and INT8.
[02:46] Samir: We compare FP16 baseline, 8-bit dynamic (we call it int8-dyn), and a more aggressive 4-bit/QLoRA-ish config for latency/cost. We measure both latency and a suite of quality tests: BLEU-like for code tasks, Rouge for summarization, and pairwise human evals on a small set.
[03:05] Sofia: That human eval piece is heavy. Can we metricize regressions?
[03:09] Lina: We instrument a quality delta metric — prompt-level KL divergence approximations and token-level perplexity delta. It's not perfect but it surfaces regressions.
[03:18] Ravi: Network: if we do VPC peering to dedicated pools, whats the typical additional latency?
[03:23] Samir: In our benchs we've seen added network hops add 2-8 ms median, but it depends on region and peering setup. We usually provision bench runs in same AZ/region to minimize variance.
[03:35] Carlos: Are there known issues when running on-prem with our NVLink config?
[03:39] Samir: We ask for a hardware spec sheet — GPU type, interconnect, driver versions. Some kernels prefer A100 vs H100 for certain sequence lengths. We'll generate a kernel-selection matrix as part of the run.
[03:52] Jordan: I'd like to walk through a sample workload. We propose three workloads: short-chat (mean 40 tokens), long-form generation (mean 600 tokens), and retrieval-augmented chat (RAG) with small context windows. Each will have a load profile: ramp to target QPS over 5 minutes, steady 20 minutes, then a burst/pulse test.
[04:18] Carlos: For RAG, is the index/hits deterministic? We need the same vector DB behavior across runs.
[04:24] Samir: We'll supply a synthetic index snapshot and a fixed set of retrieval queries, and align DB embeddings by seeding the embedder.
[04:33] Sofia: Regarding batching, do you test micro-batch sizes? We saw throughput go up but tail latency worsened.
[04:40] Lina: Yes, we include a sweep: batch sizes 1, 4, 8, 16, plus adaptive batching thresholds. We measure p50/p95/p99 latencies and cost per 1M tokens. We also instrument queue depths.
[04:56] Ravi: What's the measuring point for latency? Client-side to client-ack, or server-side token emission?
[05:01] Samir: We capture both: client-observed end-to-end, and server internal timing (kernel, kv-cache hit/miss, batch scheduling). That lets us separate network noise.
[05:12] Carlos: How do you keep the runs fair for hosted vs dedicated? Tokenization, model weights, warmup sequences — lots of noise.
[05:20] Jordan: Key is deterministic seeds, identical model binaries (we ship same model checkpoint to dedicated and on-prem), same tokenizer, same warmup script and same RNG seeds. We also pin CPU affinity and container resource limits to be consistent.
[05:34] Sofia: Any gotchas around quantized weights and GPU kernels?
[05:38] Samir: Yes — some quantization pipelines change operator ordering which affects perf. Also INT8 kernels are hardware-specific; on H100 we see different perf than A100. We'll document kernel versions and include a kernel selector in the run artifacts.
[05:53] Carlos: For evaluation, you mentioned human evals earlier — timeline is a concern. Can we do automated proxies first?
[05:59] Lina: We recommend a two-tier approach: automated proxies (KL/Perp/ROUGE) for initial sweep, then a focused human eval on the top N configurations. That reduces load for human raters.
[06:12] Ravi: Logging and PII — we need to ensure logs scrub PII and that audit logs are retained in our Vault. Can Redwood support an on-prem log sink?
[06:21] Jordan: Yes, for dedicated and private deployments we can stream logs to your s3-compatible bucket or to a private syslog. We'll include KMS/HSM options for keys.
[06:31] Carlos: Ok, let's talk measurement cadence. How granular are token-level timings?
[06:36] Samir: We capture per-token kernel timings and batch scheduling times at millisecond granularity. We also emit aggregated histograms for p50/p95/p99. For storage, we push compressed traces to the shared bucket.
[06:49] Sofia: What's the typical storage size for traces?
[06:52] Lina: For a 1M-token run traces are ~50-200MB compressed depending on sampling. We'll cap sampling for long runs.
[07:04] Jordan: Quick pivot — we built a small reproducible kit. It's a docker image with the load-generator, tokenizer parity, prompt sets, and a runner that emits a run manifest. We'll share it.
[07:15] Carlos: Great. Can you show a sample run manifest?
[07:18] Samir: (screen share described) Example fields: model_checkpoint, tokenizer_hash, seed_list_uri, warmup_length, batch_size, qps_profile, kv_warmup_script, quant_config.
[07:30] Ravi: For VPC peering we need a runbook for port 443 and if you're using private IPs we need to make sure TLS termination is handled on your side.
[07:39] Jordan: Noted. We'll include network diagrams.
[07:43] Carlos: Let's do an example result — show me an expected delta between hosted FP16 and dedicated INT8 for long-form.
[07:50] Samir: Typical reductions: INT8 can drop latency 20-40% and cost per token by ~30-50% depending on sequence length, but quality delta can be 1-3% on automated metrics; human diffs vary. We always recommend a smoke test and human spot checks.
[08:08] Sofia: Are there fallback policies? Like if INT8 has a quality regression we auto-fallback to FP16?
[08:12] Lina: Yes, Redwood supports auto-fallback policies in the routing layer — you can route based on quality gates or error rates.
[08:19] Carlos: How long to provision a dedicated pilot pool?
[08:23] Jordan: Typically 3-5 business days if we have capacity; for VPC peering add 1-2 days for networking.
[08:29] Ravi: What about on-prem deployments? Air-gapped installation timelines?
[08:33] Samir: On-prem can take 2-4 weeks depending on procurement and local ops. We have an air-gapped bundle and an install runbook.
[08:42] Carlos: Let's nail success criteria: p95 < 250 ms for short-chat, cost < $X per million tokens for short-chat, quality delta < 2% for quantized. Does that sound reasonable?
[08:54] Lina: Sounds reasonable as a starting point. We'll make them configurable for the run.
[08:59] Jordan: Ok — going into the nuts and bolts of the load script. We recommend using a closed-loop generator that keeps client concurrency fixed so you control latency pressure; open-loop (fire-and-forget) tends to blow up queueing which is not comparable.
[09:15] Carlos: So closed-loop for latency-sensitive, open-loop for stress throughput?
[09:18] Samir: Exactly. And for apples-to-apples, run both and compare.
[09:23] Sofia: A question about seed lists — how big? We were thinking 10k prompts per workload.
[09:28] Lina: 10k is fine. We usually do 10k for steady-state and smaller 1k sets for human evals. Make sure to partition seeds into train/dev/test and rotate seeds across runs to avoid cache bias.
[09:40] Ravi: For caching, how do you avoid cold-start bias when the hosted environment shares a global cache?
[09:44] Samir: We isolate cache namespaces per run for hosted; dedicated and on-prem run isolated caches. We also flush caches between runs or use distinct prefix hashes.
[09:54] Carlos: Any tips on measuring scheduling jitter from the runtime?
[09:58] Samir: Instrument task scheduling times, batch formation windows, and kernel enqueue times. We push those as separate metrics so you can see where time is spent.
[10:09] Jordan: Quick check — any legal/procurement blockers?
[10:12] Carlos: We're good to start pilot under an MSA addendum. We'll engage procurement after we see initial numbers.
[10:19] Sofia: On shared artifacts — can we have a private S3 folder?
[10:22] Jordan: Yes, we'll create a cross-account bucket or allow you to host and we push. We'll include a small script to upload runs.
[10:29] Ravi: Are there sample dashboards?
[10:32] Lina: Yes, we have a standard dashboard: token throughput, p50/p95/p99, cost per token, KV-hit rate, batch-size distribution, and a quality delta chart. We'll share a dashboard JSON for your Grafana.
[10:45] Carlos: One more question: do you run tests with mixed model variants for graceful degradation? Like fallback to smaller model on overload.
[10:52] Samir: Yes — the runbook includes a routing experiment where we simulate full capacity and route low-priority traffic to smaller cheaper variants. We track end-user error-rate and quality delta.
[11:04] Jordan: Ok, let's recap and confirm owners. Jordan will share the canonical prompt set and runner image. Samir will prepare KV-cache and quantization experiment configs. Apogee (Sofia/Ravi/Carlos) will provision VPC peering and confirm success criteria. We aim to run first benchmark window next week.
[11:23] Carlos: Sounds good. Any questions from the team?
[11:27] Sofia: Not from infra.
[11:29] Ravi: No.
[11:30] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the kickoff.
